title: Parthian Mesopotamia
subtitle: 141 BC – 224 AD · The Land Between the Empires — Ctesiphon the Arsacid Capital, the Wars with Rome, the End of Cuneiform, and the First Rabbis and the First Churches

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Mithridates I's conquest and the Arsacid settlement, Mithridates II at the height, the long stand-off with Rome from Carrhae to the Severan sacks, the client kingdoms of Characene, Hatra and Edessa, and the fall to Ardashir

entries.label: Mithridates I and the Parthian settlement
entries.hint: Mithridates I entered Seleucia in 141 and had himself acclaimed there; within a year the Babylonian Diaries were dating by 'Arsaces the king'. The Parthians kept almost everything as they found it — the Greek city and its constitution, the temple assemblies, the satrapal machinery — and added little but a garrison and a share of the revenue. It was the Achaemenid light hand a third time over.
entries.note: The Astronomical Diaries for 141 BC; Justin XXXVI.1 and XLI.6; Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Ancient Persia' (2001).

entries.label: Mithridates II the Great — the height of the empire
entries.hint: Mithridates II pushed the frontier to the Euphrates, brought Characene, Adiabene and Armenia to heel, took the old title 'King of Kings', and in 96 received the first Roman envoy, Sulla, on the Euphrates. In his reign the first silk caravans from Han China reached Parthian territory. After him a forty-year tangle of rival kings weakened the centre and let the vassal kingdoms grow.
entries.note: Justin XXXVIII.3 and XLII.2; Plutarch, 'Sulla' 5; the Chinese account of Anxi in the 'Shiji' 123.

entries.label: Orodes II — Carrhae and the wars with Rome begin
entries.hint: In 53 BC the proconsul Crassus crossed the Euphrates to conquer Parthia and was annihilated at Carrhae by a much smaller force under the general Surenas: seven legions destroyed, Crassus killed, the eagles taken. Orodes's son Pacorus then invaded Roman Syria in 40 and was thrown back and killed. The three-century contest for Mesopotamia had begun, and it would not end while either empire stood.
entries.note: Plutarch, 'Crassus' 23–31; Cassius Dio XL.12–27; Justin XLII.4.

entries.label: Phraates IV to Vologases I — the long stand-off
entries.hint: Phraates IV returned the captured eagles to Augustus in 20 BC and the two empires settled into an armed peace punctuated by wars over Armenia. Under Vologases I the arrangement hardened: a Parthian prince on the Armenian throne, crowned by Rome. Through these decades Seleucia rose against the crown for seven years, an autonomy the Arsacids could not simply crush.
entries.note: 'Res Gestae Divi Augusti' 29; Tacitus, 'Annals' VI.31–44 and XV; the 'Anilaeus and Asinaeus' episode in Josephus, 'Antiquities' XVIII.9.

entries.label: Osroes I and the Trajanic war
entries.hint: In 116 Trajan came down the Euphrates and the Tigris, took Ctesiphon, sailed to the Persian Gulf, and declared the provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria — the one time Rome held the whole land. It collapsed at once: the cities and the Jewish diaspora rose in his rear, the garrisons were cut off, and Hadrian on his accession in 117 gave the conquest back and set the border on the Euphrates again.
entries.note: Cassius Dio LXVIII.26–33; the 'Kitos War' in Eusebius, 'Ecclesiastical History' IV.2; Fergus Millar, 'The Roman Near East' (1993).

entries.label: Vologases IV to Artabanus IV — the sacks and the fall
entries.hint: Twice more Roman armies burned the capital region — Avidius Cassius in 165, Septimius Severus in 198 — each time withdrawing, each time leaving the north a little more Roman. Then the blow came from within: Ardashir, the vassal king of Persis, beat the last Arsacid, Artabanus IV, on the plain of Hormozdgan in April 224. The Parthian empire was finished after four and a half centuries.
entries.note: Cassius Dio LXXI–LXXX; Herodian VI.2; the Sasanian account in al-Tabari I (tr. Bosworth 1999).

entries.label: Characene at the head of the Gulf
entries.hint: On the marshy delta where the rivers met the sea, an officer named Hyspaosines founded a kingdom in the wreck of the late Seleucid east, with its capital at Charax. Characene minted its own coinage for three centuries, sat astride the sea route to India, and drew the Palmyrene caravan trade to its wharves. It was the most durable of the buffer states, annexed only when Ardashir swept the Gulf in 222.
entries.note: Pliny, 'Natural History' VI.31; Monika Schuol, 'Die Charakene' (2000); the Characene royal coin series.

entries.label: Hatra, Edessa and Adiabene — the buffer principalities
entries.hint: Between the two empires lay a belt of small kingdoms under Arsacid overlordship: Hatra, an Arab desert city grown rich on its shrine and its position, whose walls turned back both Trajan and Severus; Edessa, the Abgarid capital where Syriac letters began; and Adiabene around Arbela, whose royal house converted to Judaism in the first century. Rome absorbed them one by one from 165 on.
entries.note: Cassius Dio LXVIII.31 and LXXVI.10–12 (Hatra); the Adiabene conversion in Josephus, 'Antiquities' XX.2–4; Steven Ross, 'Roman Edessa' (2001).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The destruction of Crassus at Carrhae, the Parthian thrust into Syria, the seven-year revolt of Seleucia, Trajan's sack of Ctesiphon and the Jewish war in the rear, the burning of Seleucia in 165, and the Sasanian revolt

entries.label: Carrhae — the destruction of Crassus
entries.hint: Crassus led seven legions across the Euphrates in search of a triumph. On the open plain near Carrhae the Parthian general Surenas surrounded them with horse-archers and a camel train of spare arrows and shot them to pieces over a long day. Some twenty thousand Romans died and ten thousand were marched east as captives; the legionary eagles were carried to Ctesiphon. It was Rome's worst defeat in the East.
entries.note: Plutarch, 'Crassus' 23–31; Cassius Dio XL.17–27.

entries.label: The Parthian thrust into Syria and the recoil
entries.hint: With Rome in civil war the Parthians struck west: Pacorus and the Roman renegade Labienus overran Syria and pushed into Anatolia and Judaea in 40. Mark Antony's lieutenant Ventidius then beat them in three battles, killing Pacorus at Gindarus in 38 on the anniversary of Carrhae. Antony's own great invasion of 36 failed in Media with heavy loss. The frontier settled back on the Euphrates.
entries.note: Cassius Dio XLVIII.24–27 and XLIX.19–33; Plutarch, 'Antony' 33–52.

entries.label: The seven-year revolt of Seleucia
entries.hint: Seleucia threw off Arsacid control for seven years during a disputed succession, its Greek and Syrian citizens uniting against the crown — and, at the height of it, turning on the city's large Jewish community and massacring thousands. The Parthians recovered the city only by concession. It was the last time the old Greek megacity acted as an independent power, and the beginning of its long decline.
entries.note: Tacitus, 'Annals' XI.8–9; Josephus, 'Antiquities' XVIII.9.8–9.

entries.label: Trajan takes Ctesiphon, and the rear catches fire
entries.hint: Trajan stormed down the two rivers, entered Ctesiphon in 116, and reached the Gulf. Behind him every conquered city rose, and the Jewish communities of Mesopotamia, Cyrene and Egypt exploded into a war of their own. Trajan's generals retook the cities with massacres; the emperor died in 117 with the campaign unravelling, and Hadrian abandoned the whole eastern conquest within months.
entries.note: Cassius Dio LXVIII.28–33; Eusebius, 'Ecclesiastical History' IV.2; the papyrological evidence for the diaspora revolt.

entries.label: The burning of Seleucia in the war of Verus
entries.hint: Answering a Parthian move on Syria, Roman armies under Avidius Cassius drove to the Tigris. Seleucia opened its gates and was sacked and burned anyway — a betrayal the sources note — and the palace at Ctesiphon was levelled. The great Greek city never recovered. The returning legions carried a pestilence, the Antonine Plague, that killed for a decade across the whole Roman world.
entries.note: Cassius Dio LXXI.2; the 'Historia Augusta', 'Lucius Verus' 8; on the plague, Galen and R. J. Littman & M. L. Littman (1973).

entries.label: The Severan sacks and the Sasanian revolt
entries.hint: Septimius Severus sacked Ctesiphon in 198, enslaved a hundred thousand, and made the north a Roman province — but failed twice under the walls of Hatra. Caracalla attacked again in 216 and was murdered. Then Ardashir, king of Persis, rose against his Arsacid overlord and destroyed Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan in 224. Two years later he took Ctesiphon and the Sasanian age began.
entries.note: Cassius Dio LXXV–LXXIX; Herodian VI.2; al-Tabari I (tr. Bosworth 1999).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The King of Kings and the loose confederation of the great houses, the twin cities of Ctesiphon and Seleucia, the Greek self-government of Seleucia preserved, the temple assemblies still meeting, and the shift from clay to parchment

entries.label: The King of Kings and the great houses
entries.hint: The Arsacid empire was a confederation, not a state. The King of Kings held the centre and the road; around him a handful of noble clans — the Suren, the Karin and the rest — held hereditary offices and armies, and a ring of vassal kings ran their own affairs and coinage. There was no salaried bureaucracy and no standing army beyond the royal guard. It worked for four centuries and left the Sasanians much to centralise.
entries.note: Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Ancient Persia' (2001); the noble houses in the 'Letter of Tansar' and al-Tabari.

entries.label: Ctesiphon rises across the river from Seleucia
entries.hint: The Arsacids did not live in Greek Seleucia; they built their own residence on the east bank opposite it, and Ctesiphon grew from an army camp into the winter capital of the empire and the largest city of the region. The two settlements and their neighbours eventually fused into the sprawl the Arabs would call al-Madā'in, 'the Cities' — the seat of empire for the next eight hundred years.
entries.note: Strabo XVI.1.16; Pliny VI.30; Jens Kröger, 'Ctesiphon' in Encyclopaedia Iranica.

entries.label: Seleucia keeps its Greek constitution
entries.hint: Under Parthian suzerainty Seleucia went on governing itself as a Greek polis: an elected council, annual magistrates, its own bronze coinage stamped 'of the autonomous Seleucians', and years still counted on the Seleucid era. A Greek civic island inside an Iranian empire, it kept the arrangement for three centuries — until the Roman sack of 165 broke it for good.
entries.note: the autonomous coinage of Seleucia; Tacitus, 'Annals' VI.42; Getzel Cohen, 'The Hellenistic Settlements in the East' (2013).

entries.label: The temple assemblies still meet
entries.hint: The Esagila kept its assembly, its administrator and its accounts under the Parthians as under everyone before. A cluster of tablets from the 90s BC — the Rahimesu archive — shows the temple still collecting its rents and offerings and still dealing with a royal official who took his cut. The institution that had run Babylon's inner life since the Bronze Age was in its last generations, but it was still running.
entries.note: the Rahimesu archive (CT 49); R. J. van der Spek, 'The Šatammus of Esagila in the Seleucid and Arsacid Periods' (2000).

entries.label: Two eras on the same tablet
entries.hint: Parthian rule changed the dating formulae and little else: scribes now wrote the year twice, once on the old Seleucid count and once on the Arsacid era that ran from 247 BC, and named 'Arsaces' alongside the reigning king. The law, the contracts, the temple calendar and the units of measure all carried on. The lightest of overlordships, laid over institutions a thousand years deep.
entries.note: the double-dated Late Babylonian tablets; Gerd Gropp on the Arsacid era.

entries.label: From clay to parchment and potsherd
entries.hint: As cuneiform faded, the region's paperwork moved onto perishable stuff — Aramaic deeds on parchment and papyrus, receipts on broken pottery, a few in Greek. The bilingual parchments from Avroman in the Zagros, a vineyard sale of 88 BC among them, show the new practice already fixed. Most of it has rotted; the clay tablets survive precisely because their medium was obsolete.
entries.note: the Avroman parchments (E. H. Minns, JHS 1915); Sebastian Brock on the earliest Syriac legal documents.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The last cuneiform tablet and the end of the three-thousand-year tradition, the exilarch and the first Babylonian rabbis, the first churches at Edessa and Ctesiphon, the old gods of Babylon and Hatra, and the baptising sects of the lower canals

entries.label: The last cuneiform tablet
entries.hint: The youngest cuneiform tablet that can be dated is an astronomical almanac computed for the Seleucid year equivalent to AD 79/80, written in the Esagila. After it the wedge-script — three thousand years of kings, contracts, prayers, omens and star-tables — simply stops. A handful of scholars kept reading the old tablets for a while longer; no one wrote new ones.
entries.note: Hermann Hunger & Teije de Jong, 'Almanac W22340a from Uruk: The Latest Datable Cuneiform Tablet' (ZA 2014); M. J. Geller, 'The Last Wedge' (1997).

entries.label: The exilarch and the first Babylonian rabbis
entries.hint: The Arsacids recognised a head of the Jewish community — the exilarch, claiming descent from David — who held courts, levied dues and represented the Jews to the crown. Around him the first Babylonian teachers appear: Judah ben Bathyra with a school at Nisibis, a steady traffic of scholars to and from Judaea. The autonomy and the learning that would make Babylonia the centre of the Jewish world were taking shape.
entries.note: Josephus, 'Antiquities' XVIII and XX; Isaiah Gafni, 'The Jews of Babylonia in the Talmudic Era' (1990); Jacob Neusner, 'A History of the Jews in Babylonia' vol. I (1965).

entries.label: The first churches at Edessa and Adiabene
entries.hint: Christianity entered Mesopotamia early, moving along the trade roads and through the synagogues of the Aramaic-speaking towns. Edessa had a church and a bishop by the later second century, with the philosopher Bardaisan at the royal court; Adiabene and the district of Arbela had communities too. It was the first Christianity to grow up entirely outside the Roman Empire, in Syriac from the start.
entries.note: the 'Chronicle of Edessa'; Sebastian Brock, 'The Church of the East in the Sasanian Empire' (2000); Walter Bauer on Edessene Christianity.

entries.label: Bel, Nabu and Nanaya carry on
entries.hint: The old cults outlasted their script. Marduk was still honoured at Babylon and was carried by merchants to Palmyra, where he got a great temple as Bel; Nabu kept his at Borsippa; and at Uruk a Parthian-style temple to Nanaya and her consort Gareus was built as late as 110 AD. The gods were taking Hellenised and Aramaic forms, but the sanctuaries of the third millennium were still receiving offerings.
entries.note: the Gareus temple at Uruk; the cult of Bel at Palmyra (dedicated AD 32); Michael Sommer, 'Palmyra' (2018).

entries.label: Hatra of Shamash
entries.hint: Hatra was in effect a temple-state: a vast circular sanctuary at the centre of the walled city, dedicated to the sun god Shamash and the triad the inscriptions call Our Lord, Our Lady and the Son of Our Lord, drawing pilgrims and offerings from the whole steppe. The wealth of the shrine paid for the walls that twice turned back Rome. When the Sasanians finally took the city around 240 they left it to the desert.
entries.note: the Hatran Aramaic inscriptions; Lucinda Dirven (ed.), 'Hatra: Politics, Culture and Religion between Parthia and Rome' (2013).

entries.label: The baptising sects of the lower canals
entries.hint: The marshy canal country south of Ctesiphon bred a cluster of baptising sects — communities that practised repeated ritual immersion and mixed Jewish, Christian, Iranian and old Babylonian ideas. Mani, born there in 216 into an Elchasaite group, would grow up inside this world before breaking with it. The Mandaeans, who survive on those same rivers today, trace their beginnings to it.
entries.note: the 'Cologne Mani Codex'; Kevin van Bladel, 'From Sasanian Mandaeans to Ṣābians of the Marshes' (2017).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The final colophons in cuneiform, the rise of Syriac as a literary language, Parthian frontal art and the sculpture of Hatra, the rebuilt showcase cities, and the Chaldean astrology handbooks in Greek

entries.label: The last colophons in cuneiform
entries.hint: In the temple schools of Babylon and Uruk a shrinking circle of scholars kept copying the star-tables, the omen series and the classics, signing each tablet with a colophon that named the copyist and his teacher. The Graeco-Babyloniaca exercises — cuneiform on one side, Greek letters on the other — are from these last generations. When the copying ended the written culture of ancient Mesopotamia ended with it.
entries.note: Philippe Clancier, 'Les bibliothèques en Babylonie' (2009); the Graeco-Babyloniaca in M. J. Geller (1997).

entries.label: Syriac becomes a written language
entries.hint: The Aramaic dialect of Edessa began to be written in its own cursive script — the earliest dated example is a tomb inscription of AD 6 — and by the early third century it had legal documents, a Bible translation in progress, and Bardaisan's dialogue on fate and free will, the first work of Syriac prose. This local literature would carry Christianity across Persia, Central Asia and India.
entries.note: H. J. W. Drijvers & J. F. Healey, 'The Old Syriac Inscriptions of Edessa and Osrhoene' (1999); Bardaisan, 'The Book of the Laws of Countries'.

entries.label: Parthian frontality
entries.hint: Parthian art turned its figures to face the viewer head-on, standing stiff and symmetrical, eyes forward — gods, kings and donors alike. It is everywhere at Hatra and Dura-Europos, in stone, stucco and paint. The convention spread west into Roman provincial sculpture and, through it, into the frontal saints and Christs of Byzantine and medieval art. A Mesopotamian way of showing the sacred outlived the empire that made it.
entries.note: Daniel Schlumberger, 'L'Orient hellénisé' (1970); Malcolm Colledge, 'Parthian Art' (1977).

entries.label: The showcase cities in stone and stucco
entries.hint: The Parthian centuries left a distinctive built decoration: the carved stone statues and temple facades of Hatra, the moulded gypsum stucco that sheathed the walls at reoccupied Assur and at Ctesiphon, and the mass-produced terracottas and stamped sealings still turned out at Seleucia. The vocabulary mixed Greek acanthus, Iranian motifs and Semitic dress into something the region had not made before.
entries.note: Walter Andrae & Heinz Lenzen, 'Die Partherstadt Assur' (1933); Antonio Invernizzi on Seleucia.

entries.label: The Chaldean handbooks in Greek
entries.hint: By the Roman imperial period 'Chaldean' astrology circulated as Greek textbooks — the works going under the name of Teucer of Babylon among them — laying out the zodiac, the decans, the rising-times and the readings. The Babylonian doctrine had been fully absorbed into a Mediterranean science, and Babylon itself had become its legendary home rather than its working centre.
entries.note: Franz Boll, 'Sphaera' (1903); Tamsyn Barton, 'Ancient Astrology' (1994).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The last Babylonian astronomers and their almanacs, Ptolemy building the Almagest on their observations, astrology as a Roman science, the world of the Babylonian Talmud taking shape, and the incantation-bowl tradition

entries.label: The observatory winds down
entries.hint: The Esagila scholars kept up the nightly watch and the predictive almanacs into the first century AD, then stopped. Roman writers still named the Babylonians Naburimannu and Kidinnu as the founders of the lunar theories the whole world now used. Two and a half millennia of continuous sky-records — the longest scientific project in history — reached its end here, quietly, for want of successors.
entries.note: Pliny, 'Natural History' II.6; the latest Diaries and almanacs in Sachs & Hunger and in Hunger & de Jong (2014).

entries.label: Ptolemy builds the Almagest on Babylonian data
entries.hint: Ptolemy's 'Almagest', the book that fixed astronomy for fourteen centuries, rests on a Babylonian footing: eclipse observations reaching back to 721 BC, the sexagesimal number system, the 360-degree circle, and the period relations for the moon and planets — most of it reaching him through Hipparchus. The Mesopotamian achievement was now embedded in the Greek synthesis that would carry it forward.
entries.note: G. J. Toomer (tr.), 'Ptolemy's Almagest' (1984); Alexander Jones, 'The Adaptation of Babylonian Methods in Greek Numerical Astronomy' (1991).

entries.label: Astrology becomes a universal science
entries.hint: By the imperial period the horoscope was cast from Roman Britain to India, and its framework — the zodiac, the twelve places, the aspects, the planetary rulerships — was Babylonian to the core, refined by Greek geometry. Mesopotamia was remembered as its birthplace even as its own practitioners fell silent. It is the most widely practised legacy of ancient Babylon, and still is.
entries.note: Dorotheus of Sidon, 'Carmen Astrologicum'; Vettius Valens, 'Anthologiae'; Francesca Rochberg, 'In the Path of the Moon' (2010).

entries.label: The oral Torah moves east
entries.hint: After the destruction of Jerusalem the centre of Jewish life began shifting toward the large, secure, self-governing community of Babylonia. Scholars carried the mishnaic material and the methods of legal argument to the schools of Nisibis and Nehardea, and a two-way traffic of teachers ran with Palestine. By the end of the Parthian period Babylonia was poised to become the senior seat of the law and produce the Talmud that bears its name.
entries.note: Jacob Neusner, 'A History of the Jews in Babylonia' vol. I (1965); Isaiah Gafni, 'Land, Center and Diaspora' (1997).

entries.label: The exorcist's craft outlives the script
entries.hint: The lore of the Babylonian āšipu — the incantations, the protective figurines, the demon-names Lilith and Lamashtu, the rites against sickness and the evil eye — did not stop when cuneiform did. It passed into the Aramaic magical practice of Jews, Mandaeans and Christians in the same towns, and surfaces a few centuries later on the inscribed clay bowls buried under house floors across Iraq.
entries.note: Markham Geller, 'Ancient Babylonian Medicine' (2010); Shaul Shaked & others, 'Aramaic Bowl Spells' (2013– ).
